places.history_en: Taipei 101 is the 508-metre tower at the centre of Xinyi, with 101 floors above ground and five basements. Ground was broken in January 1999, the mall podium was completed in November 2003, and the tower officially opened on 31 December 2004. Architects C.Y. Lee and C.P. Wang stacked eight flared segments of eight floors each, a number tied to good fortune, and repeated curled ruyi shapes and coin discs on the outside. Indoor observatories are on floors 88 and 89, with outdoor decks on 91 and 101. It has hosted the city's New Year fireworks since the first seconds of 2005.

places.zh: 台北101風阻尼器與觀景台
places.en: Taipei 101 tuned mass damper and observatory
places.years: In service since the tower opened, 2004-12-31; 101st-floor outdoor deck opened 2019-06-14
places.history_en: Near the top of Taipei 101 hangs a 660-tonne steel ball that visitors can walk up to. It is a tuned mass damper: a pendulum that swings against the tower's own sway in typhoons and earthquakes. The ball is 5.5 metres across, built from 41 stacked steel plates each 125 mm thick, and hangs between the 92nd and 88th floors, where the indoor observatory lets people look straight at it. Sanrio designed five Damper Baby mascots for it. After the April 2024 Hualien earthquake, news outlets worldwide pointed to this ball as the reason the tower came through.
places.history_zh: 台北101的風阻尼器是一顆重660公噸、直徑5.5公尺的鋼球，由41片鋼板疊成，懸吊於92樓至88樓之間，颱風與地震時反向擺動以減少大樓搖晃，遊客可在觀景台近距離觀看。

places.history_en: The red LOVE sculpture outside Taipei 101 is one of the versions of American pop artist Robert Indiana's best-known work: the letters L and O stacked over V and E, with the O tilted. The original three-dimensional LOVE dates from about 1970 and was made in weathering steel; copies stand in cities around the world. One commentary says the Taipei piece arrived with the tower's opening in 2004. It became the default meeting point and photo spot at the foot of the tower, and news photos from 2026 still show tourists queueing to pose in front of it.

places.en: Vieshow Cinemas Taipei Xinyi (formerly Warner Village)
places.years: Opened 1998-01-24 as 華納威秀; renamed 威秀影城 in 2006; still open
places.history_en: Xinyi Vieshow opened on 24 January 1998 as Warner Village, a joint venture between Warner Bros. and Australia's Village Roadshow, when much of the Xinyi planning zone was still empty lots. Many Taipei people still call it by the old name. The two foreign partners left in 2004 and the company became Vieshow Cinemas in 2006. It is the chain's first site and its only stand-alone building, with 15 halls today, and Taiwan's first 4DX hall opened here in 2013. Film fans call it movie-lover's heaven because premieres, the Taipei Film Festival and the Golden Horse festival use it. A planned 2019 closure was replaced by a ten-year lease renewal.

places.history_en: Shin Kong Mitsukoshi's Xinyi Place is four department-store buildings that opened in stages: A11 in November 1997, A8 in January 2002, A9 in December 2003 and A4 in September 2005. A11 was the first big store in the planning zone, and the four together turned the area into Taipei's main shopping district. They are joined by skybridges and underground passages, with plazas between them. The pedestrian strip that runs between the buildings, Xiangti Avenue, is where the Christmas lights go up each winter and where the city licenses fixed pitches for street performers, including one between A8 and A9.

places.history_en: The Xinyi skywalk is a network of raised walkways at second-floor level that lets people cross the district without touching the road. One news report counts it as linking eleven department stores and one cinema over about 2.3 kilometres, and calls it the densest footbridge system in Taiwan. It runs from Taipei 101 north through ATT 4 FUN, Vieshow and the Shin Kong Mitsukoshi buildings, on past Breeze Songgao, and reaches Breeze Xinyi at Zhongxiao East Road. Most sections are open all day; the bridge into Taipei 101 passes through the building, so it follows metro hours, 6 a.m. to 1 a.m.

places.years: Opened 2006-01-01 at midnight; closed 2023-12-24; site reopened as Dream Plaza 2025-07-25
places.history_en: Eslite's Xinyi flagship opened at midnight on 1 January 2006 with about 8,000 square metres of floor space, then the largest bookstore in Taiwan. When the Dunnan store closed on 31 May 2020, Xinyi took over as the chain's only bookstore open 24 hours, and a generation of night readers sat on its floors. The landlord, Uni-President Group, did not renew the lease, and the store closed on Christmas Eve, 24 December 2023, after 18 years. The all-night bookstore moved to Eslite Spectrum Songyan on 20 January 2024. The building at No. 11 Songgao Road has since reopened as Uni-President's Dream Plaza mall.

places.zh: 四四南村（信義公民會館）
places.en: Four Four South Village (Xinyi Assembly Hall)
places.years: Built 1948 (infobox says 1949); fire 1999; relocation settled 2001; registered historic building 2003-12-23
places.history_en: Four Four South Village was housing for the workers of the 44th Arsenal, who came to Taipei from the mainland in the late 1940s. It took its name from standing south of the arsenal. Families lived in joined single-storey rows laid out like fish bones, each home under ten ping, at first without running water or private toilets. A fire in 1999 led to clearance and the relocation was settled in 2001, but a few rows were kept and registered as a historic building on 23 December 2003. They now hold the Xinyi Assembly Hall and a village museum. The low tiled roofs with Taipei 101 rising behind them are one of the district's best-known contrasts.

places.en: Xiangshan (Elephant Mountain) trail and Six Giant Rocks viewpoint
places.years: Natural hill; trail in use (opening year unknown — needs CJ)
places.history_en: Xiangshan, or Elephant Mountain, is the 184-metre sandstone hill just south-east of Taipei 101. A stepped trail climbs its western slope and ridge, and the walk to the top takes about half an hour. Partway up, a cluster of boulders known as the Six Giant Rocks gives the postcard view: the whole Xinyi skyline with Taipei 101 dead centre. Photographers line the platforms at dusk, and on New Year's Eve people claim spots hours ahead to watch the fireworks. The easiest way in is from Xiangshan metro station, Exit 2, then straight ahead to the trailhead off Xinyi Road Section 5.

places.zh: 台北市政府大樓與市民廣場
places.en: Taipei City Hall and Citizen Plaza
places.history_en: Taipei City Hall has anchored the north end of the Xinyi planning zone since 1994, years before the malls arrived. Construction began on 6 June 1986. The building has twelve floors above ground and two below, and from the air its plan forms two crosses side by side, the character for ten written twice, a nod to Double Ten day; the shape also lets light and air into the offices. It regularly hosts exhibitions, performances and public events. The open plaza in front is where the city stages its New Year's Eve countdown concert, with Taipei 101 as the backdrop to the south.
places.history_zh: 台北市政府大樓1986年6月6日動工、1994年落成，地上12層、地下2層，俯瞰呈「雙十」形。大樓常舉辦展覽與公共活動，前方的市民廣場是台北跨年晚會的舞台，南望即是台北101。

places.history_en: Taipei City Hall Bus Station opened on 5 August 2010 at the south-east corner of Keelung Road and Zhongxiao East Road. For many people this is where a day in Xinyi starts or ends: long-distance coaches to northern and central Taiwan leave from here, about 24,000 bus passengers pass through daily, and City Hall metro station on the Bannan Line is built into the basement. Above the bus bays is a mixed-use tower about 150 metres tall. A Uni-President department store fills nine levels, and the W Taipei hotel, which began trial operations in February 2011, takes floors 8 to 31 with 405 rooms.

places.history_en: The mall at No. 12 Songshou Road opened in March 2000 as New York New York, one of the first shopping centres in the planning zone. Its operator shut it in August 2010 after losing about NT$1.8 billion over nine years. It reopened on 29 August 2011 as ATT 4 FUN, aimed at a younger crowd, with street-fashion brands, themed restaurants, a sky lounge bar and a 2,000-seat show hall on the seventh floor. The building has ten floors above ground and three below. Second-floor skybridges tie it to Vieshow on one side and to Nan Shan Plaza and Taipei 101 on the other.

places.history_en: Taipei Nan Shan Plaza is the 272-metre, 48-storey tower that went up next door to Taipei 101 between December 2014 and June 2018, designed by the Japanese firm Mitsubishi Jisho Sekkei. It is the second tall shape in every recent skyline photo of Xinyi. The complex has three parts: the office tower, a seven-storey mall block run by Breeze Center as Breeze Nan Shan, and a diamond-shaped entrance building with about 1,600 square metres of public art space. It connects to Taipei 101, ATT 4 FUN and Vieshow by footbridge and underground passage. For people who came to Xinyi after 2019, its food floors are a regular stop.

events.history_en: Taipei 101 officially opened on 31 December 2004, five years after construction began and a little over a year after its mall was completed. At 508 metres it was the tallest building in the world at the time, a title it kept until Dubai's Burj Khalifa passed it. The opening week was treated as a festival: a French climber scaled the tower on Christmas Day as part of the programme, and a few hours after the ceremony the building fired its first New Year fireworks. For Xinyi, the opening fixed the district's centre for good; everything built since is measured against the tower.

events.history_en: The first Taipei 101 fireworks went off on the night of 31 December 2004, a few hours after the tower's opening ceremony, to welcome 2005. Reports say the show lasted only 35 seconds and that the building paid for it itself. The year before, with the tower unfinished, the countdown had been done with lights alone. From that short burst grew the yearly show that Taiwan watches on television and that fills Xinyi's streets, the City Hall plaza and the slopes of Xiangshan with people every 31 December; later shows ran for minutes rather than seconds.

events.history_en: On Christmas Day 2004, six days before the official opening, French climber Alain Robert climbed the outside of Taipei 101. The climb was legal and invited, part of the opening week. He reached the top of the pinnacle in about four hours, double his own estimate, because heavy rain made the surface slick. A month earlier he had fallen two metres during a photo shoot and needed forty stitches in his elbow. A later news report says he used ropes on this climb. He was the first person to climb the tower, and for 21 years the only one widely remembered for it.

events.zh: 艾力克斯·霍諾德無繩攀登台北101
events.en: Alex Honnold's rope-free climb of Taipei 101
events.history_en: On Sunday 25 January 2026, American climber Alex Honnold climbed the outside of Taipei 101 with no rope and no safety gear, and reached the top of the spire. Netflix streamed it live as Skyscraper Live. The climb had been set for the day before and was pushed back one day because of the weather. Wikipedia records his time as 1 hour, 31 minutes and 43 seconds. He paused after the stacked middle section, nicknamed the bamboo boxes, to wave at onlookers. On top he took a selfie and said it was windy, then roped up for the first time to come down. The climb was authorized; he is the first person to climb the tower without a rope.

events.zh: 2021年三級警戒下的信義區空城
events.en: COVID-19 Level 3 alert: the empty streets of Xinyi
events.years: Level 3 announced for Taipei and New Taipei 2021-05-15; nationwide from 2021-05-19; lowered 2021-07-27 (end date inferred)
events.history_en: On 15 May 2021 Taiwan's epidemic command centre raised Taipei and New Taipei to a Level 3 alert, and on 19 May extended it to the whole country. There was no legal lockdown, but people stayed home anyway. The night after the announcement a photographer flew a drone over Xinyi and found the traffic and the crowds gone; public television described the district as looking like an empty city. Department stores shortened their hours, the Taipei 101 mall opened only from noon to 8 p.m. in late May, and the 89th-floor observatory closed. Some clothing shops reported sales down more than 80 percent.
events.history_zh: 2021年5月15日，雙北升為第三級警戒，19日擴及全國。民眾自主減少外出，隔日空拍的信義區夜景車潮人潮消失，宛如空城；百貨縮短營業時間，台北101觀景台也暫停開放。

events.history_en: Eslite Xinyi closed on Christmas Eve 2023, after 18 years, because its lease with landlord Uni-President Group ran out. On the last day the building was packed and staff set up queue lines to keep people moving through the shelves; public television quoted chairperson Wu Min-chieh on the memories visitors had left there. The lights went out at 10:30 p.m. A report says more than 75,000 people came on the day before. The store had been Taipei's only all-night bookstore since 2020, and that role moved to the Songshan Cultural and Creative Park branch in January 2024.

events.en: 3 April 2024 Hualien earthquake and the Taipei 101 damper
events.history_en: On the morning of 3 April 2024 a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck near Hualien on Taiwan's east coast, the strongest the island had felt in 25 years. In Taipei the towers of Xinyi swayed, and Taipei 101 stayed standing. News outlets around the world explained why by pointing to the 660-tonne steel ball near its top, which swings against the building's movement and, by the tower's own figures, can cut the sway by up to 40 percent. No source read for this file gives a measured swing for that morning. The record on file is one metre, set in a 2015 typhoon.
